g.passage: Folded twice and then once more, Salma's invitation lay on the planks of the dock where she had set it, weighted with a lemon. Her new daughter-in-law had come to Marrakesh only that spring, and the lake below the rented villa was the one corner of the household where nobody followed anyone. Each evening the bride walked to the end of the dock, unfolded the card, read the date of Salma's luncheon, and folded it again along the same creases. She did not answer it, and she did not throw it into the water. Wolfram, watching from the terrace, called the card his mother's paper anchor. Salma heard him and went on shelling beans. On the third evening the bride carried the lemon back to the kitchen, sliced it, and served it with the tea, leaving the card on the boards with nothing on top of it.

g.passage: When the ice truck stopped coming to the harbor in Colombo, Ayita began packing the morning catch in sawdust from the boatyard. Her family's stall had sold fish on the same corner for forty years, and the shutter now stuck halfway each dawn while the newer stalls rolled theirs up with a motor. Faisal, who had fished beside her grandfather, came by every morning, lifted the shutter the last few inches with his shoulder, and left without buying anything. Buyers still came, mostly old ones, and the scale still swung. One wet morning Faisal called the stall a lantern with the wick cut short. Ayita wrote the phrase on the back of a receipt. The following week she ordered a new shutter spring, then put the receipt in the cash tin beneath the coins, where she would see it each time she made change.

g.passage: Lamp oil and old glue were what I smelled first each morning in the library in Naples, where I was apprenticed to Milena the year I turned nineteen. __Every afternoon she brought me a pastry from the bakery on the corner and set it on my desk without a word.__ I was restless that year, forever asking to work in the reading room instead of the bindery, forever glancing at the door. Milena kept me at the bench, teaching me to resew spines and float torn pages. The pastries kept coming, wrapped in brown paper, and I ate them over my work and wondered whether they were apology or bribe. In the spring a collector came to inspect the library's oldest atlas. Milena showed him every repair and named each one; most were mine. He asked who had done the gathering on the fourth section, and she unfolded a square of brown pastry paper from her drawer, on which, in her small hand, she had kept a dated list of every page I had mended.
